projects.title: PeopleOps Data Warehouse
projects.meta: Practice case study · Python · T-SQL · 182k+ records
projects.summary: A six-stage HR and attendance pipeline: clean the files, keep employee history, and make rejected rows visible instead of silent.
paragraphs: PeopleOps is my main data-engineering case study. It treats HR and attendance data the way an operations team actually receives it: more than one file, inconsistent dates, attributes that change, and questions that need an answer you can defend.

I split the work into six stages so the path stays readable. Python and Pandas handle intake, light standardization and run context. SQL Server is where the model, the history and the checks live. The goal is a workflow another person could follow without asking me to narrate the notebook.

The warehouse shape is a star schema. Attendance and payroll-style events are facts. Employee, department and date are dimensions. Employee history follows an SCD Type 2 idea — effective-from, effective-to and a current-row flag — so a report can ask both “what is true now?” and “what was true then?”

Quality checks are part of the design. Typical rules are missing employee identifiers, impossible dates, duplicate business keys and events that fall outside an active window. A failed row is written to a rejection log with the reason and the run that saw it.

Loads are meant to be safe to run again. A stable business key plus a row fingerprint (_row_hash) lets an unchanged record pass through without being applied twice. That habit matters more to me, at this stage, than claiming a cloud schedule I have not operated yet.

The study references more than 182,000 records as the working volume for these patterns. The diagrams on this page are reference drawings. When a real SQL Server or terminal screenshot is ready, replace the file in public/img and keep the same image path.

projects.sqlLabel: T-SQL · example audit, not a production script
projects.sql:
-- Example only. Rename tables and columns to match the real schema.
SELECT
    e.employee_id,
    e.employee_name,
    e.separation_date,
    p.pay_period_end,
    p.net_pay,
    p.payment_reference
FROM dbo.dim_employee AS e
INNER JOIN dbo.fact_payroll AS p
    ON p.employee_key = e.employee_key
WHERE e.separation_date IS NOT NULL
  AND p.pay_period_end > e.separation_date
  AND p.net_pay > 0
ORDER BY
    e.employee_id,
    p.pay_period_end DESC;

projects.title: Python Data Utilities
projects.meta: Practice project · Python · file I/O · data cleaning
projects.summary: Small command-line tools that read messy text, filter records, and write a cleaner file — with errors handled on purpose.
paragraphs: Before a warehouse is useful, someone has to look at the file. These utilities are small Python command-line tools I wrote to filter and reshape mock structured data without opening a spreadsheet and hoping.
Each script reads from disk, checks that the file is actually there, and refuses to crash on a blank line or a short row. Bad records are reported. Good records are written out in a consistent shape.

The point of the project is habit: functions with clear inputs, basic data structures, simple object-oriented organization where it helps, and file I/O that tells you what it did. It is the same instinct I use at the front of an ETL flow.
It is a practice project, not a product. When a utility grows into something worth showing line by line, the GitHub field below is the place to point at the repository.

projects.title: PeopleOps Data Engineering Pipeline & Analytics Warehouse
projects.meta: End-to-End Case Study · Python · T-SQL · Star Schema · 182k+ Records
projects.summary: An automated 6-stage HR and attendance data pipeline featuring SCD Type 2 tracking, financial leakage auditing, and robust data quality assertions.
paragraphs: PeopleOps is an advanced data engineering case study designed to ingest messy, multi-source human resources and biometric attendance logs, transforming them into a production-ready analytical data warehouse.

The architecture flows through six explicit stages managed by Python and Microsoft SQL Server: raw extraction with programmatic row hashing for idempotency, staging cleanup, attendance rules engine, star schema dimensional modeling, executive CFO analytics, and automated data quality assertions.

By maintaining Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD) Type 2 tracking for employee histories and isolating rejected corrupt punches into dedicated audit logs, the pipeline ensures historical accuracy and data integrity across more than 182,000 processed records.

highlights: 100% idempotent loading using programmatic row hashing (_row_hash)
SCD Type 2 history tracking for employee department and attribute changes

Rigorous automated Data Quality assertions across all warehouse layers
projects.sqlLabel: T-SQL · CFO Financial Leakage Audit Query
projects.sql:
-- Detect salary payments made after an employee's resignation date
WITH SeparatedEmployees AS (
    SELECT 
        employee_id,
        resignation_date
    FROM warehouse.dim_employee
    WHERE resignation_date IS NOT NULL 
      AND is_current = 1
)
SELECT 
    p.employee_id,
    p.pay_date,
    p.net_salary,
    e.resignation_date
FROM raw_payroll AS p
INNER JOIN SeparatedEmployees AS e 
    ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id
WHERE p.pay_date > e.resignation_date
ORDER BY p.pay_date DESC;
